archetype.name: Fringe Contender (defense-first)
archetype.definition: A league-average team by net efficiency that wins because its pass defense is top-five, it rarely beats itself, and it keeps games close enough to steal, while an inefficient passing game caps how high it can go.

report.headline: A good defense and a misused run game keep winning the close ones.
report.take:
Pittsburgh at 4-2 is the team it has been for most of this decade. Net EPA sits 17th, almost exactly where it finished in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and the record again runs a little ahead of the play: 0.83 wins over expected, with the point differential implying 3.2 wins rather than four. That gap is small and fully in character. The history shows a positive wins-over-expected figure every season since 2020, so this is not a fluke so much as a style. They play clean (3rd fewest penalties, 2nd fewest line penalties), hold the ball (7th in time of possession), win 75% of one-score games and let the defense close.

The defense is the engine. It ranks 6th in EPA allowed and 5th against the pass, 6th on third down and 7th in the red zone. How it gets there is unusual: it ranks dead last in pressure rate, yet 5th in EPA allowed on short passes. This is a coverage-and-tackle-the-catch unit that suffocates the underneath game. The 16 sacks, 9th in the league, sit oddly next to that pressure rate, and five of them came in one game at Tampa Bay. Expect that number to cool. The cracks are the ones a low-pressure, sit-back defense usually has: explosive passes allowed rank 27th and the missed-tackle rate ranks 29th. The schedule has also been kind. Most opponents rank as middling or worse offenses today, and the one top-ten attack it faced, Cincinnati, scored 27.

The offense is where the numbers argue with the play-calling. The run game is genuinely good: 4.75 yards a carry (3rd), run EPA 5th, a perfect short-yardage conversion rate. Yet Pittsburgh passes 5.5 points above expectation, the 3rd-highest rate in football, with a passing game 26th in EPA. Aaron Rodgers has started every game. The line actually keeps pressure down (7th), but the sack rate is 24th and time to throw 22nd, so pressures are turning into sacks at a high rate: 19 taken, including five apiece against Cleveland and Tampa Bay. The Week 2 loss at New England (3 points, -21.8 pass EPA) showed how bad it gets when the passing game stalls and drags the rest down with it.

That matters more now because the receiver room is thin. Michael Pittman Jr. (78% of snaps) and Roman Wilson (25 targets) are on injured reserve with mid-to-late-November return estimates, and Ben Skowronek is out. DK Metcalf and Germie Bernard carry the wideout load, with Jaylen Warren and Pat Freiermuth as the other volume targets. The sensible correction is to lean harder on Warren and the ground game until Pittman is back. Whether they do will decide whether this stays a 10-win team or slips toward the middle of a crowded AFC North.

strengths.title: Pass defense that erases underneath throws
strengths.body: Pittsburgh ranks 5th in pass EPA allowed and 5th on short passes despite generating the least pressure in the league. It wins with coverage and rallying to the catch, which also shows up on third down (6th) and in the red zone (7th). Coverage-driven numbers tend to hold better than pressure-driven ones, though the opponents so far have mostly been average or weaker offenses.

strengths.title: A ground game that actually works
strengths.body: Run EPA ranks 5th and yards per carry 3rd, with Jaylen Warren taking the bulk of carries and a 100% short-yardage conversion rate. Yards before contact are only 21st, so the backs are creating a good share of it themselves. That is a bit less bankable than line-driven success, but the stuff rate (9th) says the front is holding up.

strengths.title: Clean, possession-heavy football
strengths.body: Few penalties, a positive turnover differential of 3 and the 7th-best time of possession keep games short and close. That is the mechanism behind a 75% one-score win rate and a long run of beating the point differential. It is a repeatable habit more than luck, though close-game records always wobble.

concerns.title: Passing too much, passing poorly
concerns.body: The offense throws at the 3rd-highest rate over expectation while its pass EPA ranks 26th, the clearest misallocation on the team. With Pittman and Wilson on IR, the receiving corps behind Metcalf is thinner than when that tilt began. Until it shifts toward the run, the offense will keep producing stinkers like the 3-point game at New England.

concerns.title: Pressures becoming sacks
concerns.body: The line allows pressure at only the 7th-lowest rate, yet the sack rate is 24th and 19 sacks have been taken. A slow time to throw suggests holding the ball rather than a line breakdown. That points to a quarterback-and-route issue that won't fix itself without quicker answers.

concerns.title: Big plays and missed tackles
concerns.body: The cost of a sit-back, no-pressure defense is that it gives up chunks: explosive passes allowed rank 27th and missed tackles 29th. Against average offenses the short-game suffocation has covered for it. Better attacks like Cincinnati, which scored 27, and the backloaded Baltimore and Jacksonville games will test it.

trend.note: The offense climbed out of a dreadful start, with positive pass EPA from Week 3 through Week 5 and 34 points against Indianapolis. It then fell back to -13.5 pass EPA and five sacks taken at Tampa Bay, a game the defense won. The defense has been the steady part: no opponent has topped 27.

nextGame.headline: The league's worst run defense meets one of its best run games
nextGame.body:
Pittsburgh is a 3.5-point favorite (-185) against a 2-4 New Orleans team that ranks 28th in net EPA and 27th in EPA allowed. The Saints defense ranks last in rush EPA allowed and last in success rate allowed, generates little pressure (29th) and is 31st on deep passes. That is exactly the profile that should let Pittsburgh run and keep Rodgers upright. The Saints offense under Tyler Shough is middling by EPA (20th) but scores 25.3 a game. Its run game is weak (3.39 yards a carry), which plays into a Steelers defense whose strength is shutting down the pass. The game is indoors, and the injury notes have the Saints traveling to Paris for it, so the road label may matter less than usual.

Availability tilts toward Pittsburgh. New Orleans is without linebacker Kaden Elliss (100% of snaps), defensive tackle Nathan Shepherd and linebacker Anfernee Jennings, which hollows out the run defense further. Both starting corners, Kool-Aid McKinstry and Quincy Riley, are questionable, as is guard Cesar Ruiz. Pittsburgh's problem is at receiver: Pittman and Wilson are on IR and Skowronek is out, leaving Metcalf, Bernard, Freiermuth and Warren to carry the passing game. Safety DeShon Elliott is on IR with a return estimate of this week, and backup corner Brandin Echols is questionable.

waysToWin.title: Feed Warren against a broken run defense
waysToWin.body: New Orleans ranks last in rush EPA allowed and success rate allowed, and it is missing Elliss and Shepherd from its front. Pittsburgh's run game ranks 5th in EPA, so this is the clearest edge on the board. Leaning into it also shortens the game and plays to the time-of-possession style.

waysToWin.title: Metcalf and Freiermuth against soft spots
waysToWin.body: Opposing WR1s score 3.1 PPR points over their average against New Orleans (26th), and tight ends see an outsized 30% of targets with high EPA per play. With the Saints' pressure rate 29th and two starting corners questionable, Rodgers should get the clean pockets his sack problem needs. Shots to Metcalf have room too, since the Saints rank 31st on deep passes.

waysToWin.title: Coverage stalls a middling offense
waysToWin.body: Pittsburgh's short-pass defense and third-down defense are both top-six. New Orleans can't lean on its run game, which ranks 26th in yards per carry. Forcing Shough into long, patient drives favors the Steelers.

waysToLose.title: Abandoning the run, taking sacks
waysToLose.body: If Pittsburgh keeps its pass-heavy tilt with a depleted receiver room, it risks another Tampa Bay-style afternoon: drive-killing sacks and negative pass EPA. The sack rate is 24th even with good protection numbers. A weak Saints pass rush only helps if the ball comes out on time.

waysToLose.title: Explosives turn it into a shootout
waysToLose.body: New Orleans scores 25.3 points a game despite mediocre efficiency, which points to chunk plays. Pittsburgh's defense allows explosive passes at the 27th-ranked rate and misses tackles often. A couple of busted coverages could flip a game the Steelers are built to win slowly.

waysToLose.title: Special teams and fourth-down gap
waysToLose.body: The Saints rank 10th in special-teams EPA per game against Pittsburgh's 21st. New Orleans goes for it on fourth down at the league's top rate, while Pittsburgh ranks 30th. In a game the Book sees as a field goal and change, hidden yardage and a couple of extra Saints possessions could decide it.

nextGame.watch: Pittsburgh's run-pass mix early: if Warren gets steady carries against the league's worst rush defense, this should play out as the Book expects; if Rodgers is throwing on early downs to a short-handed receiver group, it gets closer.

restOfSeason.body:
The schedule stiffens after New Orleans. Two games against Baltimore, plus Cincinnati, Jacksonville and Carolina, bring top-ten offenses that will test the big-play leaks. Denver and Cleveland bring good defenses that can expose the passing game. The division is a three-way tie at 4-2, so the four division games carry the season. What should hold: the pass defense's coverage-based efficiency, the run game and the clean, close-game style that has beaten the point differential every year since 2020. What should regress: the defensive sack total, given the league's lowest pressure rate, and likely a bit of the one-score magic.

The swing piece is the offense's balance. Pittman's return estimate in mid-November should help the passing game. Until then, pushing more of the offense through the run is the way to avoid stalls like New England and Tampa Bay. With an efficiency profile that has sat near the league middle for years, a 9-to-11-win finish is the realistic band. That likely lands them in the wild-card mix rather than as a clear division favorite.
swingFactors: Whether the offense shifts its balance toward the run
Pittman's and Wilson's returns from IR
The two Baltimore games and the division race

confidence.note: Six-game sample with a soft early schedule, but the profile closely matches recent seasons.
